title: git-refs push queue can drop a newer same-ref update during an in-flight push

verdict.rationale: The evidence shows the queue was designed to be durable, with entries cleared only after a confirmed push, but nothing addresses a same-ref re-enqueue during an in-flight push. Remove-by-name dropping a newer generation is an unconsidered concurrency gap, not a chosen behaviour.

Recover a diverged checkpoint ref by fetch+replay instead of leaving it queued

Build on the non-force push: when a per-checkpoint ref is rejected (it diverged
on the remote — the same checkpoint re-written elsewhere), instead of just
leaving it queued, fetch the remote ref and replay the local-only commits on top
via the existing fetchAndRebaseRefCommon, then retry. The retry stays non-force
(after the replay the local ref is a fast-forward over the remote), so the
remote's commit is preserved as an ancestor, never overwritten. The cherry-pick
is delta-based, so non-overlapping changes merge; a genuine overlap (both sides
rewrote the same file) surfaces as a rebase error and the ref is left for a later
pre-push — degrading to the previous safe behavior, never to a force overwrite.

pre-push keeps the batch push as the fast path (one round-trip when everything
fast-forwards) and falls back to this per-ref recovery only for rejected refs,
removing from the queue just those that land. Adds a test proving a diverged ref
ends up with both the remote-only and local-only changes after recovery.

fix: bound the per-ref checkpoint push fallback

When the batch push fails, the fallback retried every queued ref one at
a time, each costing at least one network round-trip, with no bound but
the 2-minute per-ref budget. A reporter with 305 queued refs saw their
git push sit for nine minutes and land 4 of them; a healthy remote would
still have taken ~16 minutes, and an unreachable one up to ten hours.
The premise does not hold either: the batch fails on divergence, but
just as often wholesale, and then no amount of per-ref recovery helps.

Stop after maxConsecutiveRefPushFailures failures in a row, an expired
checkpointFlushBudget, or a cancelled context — always after at least
one attempt, so the queue still drains a little at a time. A success
resets the count, so one blocked checkpoint cannot strand the refs
queued behind it, and skipped refs stay queued for the next push.

Also log the batch error before the fallback runs. The per-ref retries
re-derive a rejection reason, but a transport failure matches none of
them and the non-auth path does not return batchErr, so the cause of a
wholesale failure reached neither the terminal nor .entire/logs.

fix: rotate failed refs so a bounded flush stays fair

The queue drains in first-seen order and Remove preserves it, so a
bounded fallback stops at the same place on every push. A prefix that
consistently fails — five checkpoints blocked by secret scanning, say —
is therefore retried in that same order forever, and the healthy refs
behind it are never attempted at all. A pre-receive hook declines the
whole push, so the batch cannot land them either: they are stranded,
while the abort line promises another attempt next push.

That was a regression in the bound itself: walking the whole queue was
slow, but it did eventually reach them.

Rotate this flush's failures to the back of the queue, so every queued
ref eventually gets an attempt. PushQueue.Rotate does the reorder under
one lock rather than Remove plus Enqueue, which leaves a window where
the refs are in neither the queue nor the remote. Skipped after an
interruption, where the failures say nothing about the refs.

test: pin that a bounded flush also rotates on an exhausted budget

Rotation deliberately covers budget exhaustion, not just the failure
cap, and the code only said why it skips an interruption — so a reviewer
read the budget case as accidental and proposed confining rotation to
the cap. That would restore the starvation for a slow remote, which
expires the budget at roughly the same queue position on every push and
so never reaches the tail.

Rotation is fair scheduling rather than a verdict on a ref: it drops
nothing and only changes order, so a ref cut mid-flight by the deadline
losing its place costs nothing. Say that where the condition is, and pin
it with a test that fails under the narrower condition.
